title: Does LLM Pre-Training Typically Occur at the Edge of Stability?

paper.title: Does LLM Pre-Training Typically Occur at the Edge of Stability?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Quadratic approximations provide a common lens for studying neural network optimization, but recent evidence challenges their predictive validity. In full-batch gradient descent with learning rate (LR) η \eta , Cohen et al. (2021) observed the Edge of Stability (EoS), where the largest Hessian eigenvalue concentrates near 2 / η 2/\eta , seemingly at odds with classical stability conditions predicted by quadratic approximations.
In this work, we revisit the fidelity of quadratic approximations as a model of neural network training dynamics, with a particular focus on their failure modes in LLM training.
We first highlight a distinct failure mode of the quadratic approximation, where persistent negative curvature causes the quadratic dynamics to diverge regardless of the LR, even though the real dynamics remain stable.
We term this phenomenon the Edge of Convexity (EoC).
After removing the effect of this LR-independent instability, we then propose a generalized definition of Edge of Stability (EoS) for stochastic training with adaptive optimizers, based on whether increasing the LR induces significant divergence in the quadratic dynamics while leaving the real dynamics largely unchanged.
Across different LLM pretraining runs with various model sizes up to 787 787 M, we find that (1) EoC is always observed across LLM pretraining, and (2) EoS is also prevalent but not universal: it disappears when the LR becomes sufficiently small (e.g., after decay) or when the batch size falls below a critical threshold that has a positive correlation with the critical batch size.
Together, these findings characterize when and how quadratic approximations fail and provide a foundation for future work on understanding training dynamics.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In optimization theory, the dynamics of gradient-based methods are commonly analyzed through a local quadratic approximation of the loss function, given by the second-order Taylor expansion around the current iterate: ℒ ( 𝒘 t + 1 ) ≈ ℒ ( 𝒘 t ) + ( 𝒘 t + 1 − 𝒘 t ) ⊤ ∇ ℒ ( 𝒘 t ) + 1 2 ( 𝒘 t + 1 − 𝒘 t ) ⊤ ∇ 2 ℒ ( 𝒘 t ) ( 𝒘 t + 1 − 𝒘 t ) . \mathcal{L}(\bm{w}_{t+1})\approx\mathcal{L}(\bm{w}_{t})+(\bm{w}_{t+1}-\bm{w}_{t})^{\top}\nabla\mathcal{L}(\bm{w}_{t})+\frac{1}{2}(\bm{w}_{t+1}-\bm{w}_{t})^{\top}\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}(\bm{w}_{t})(\bm{w}_{t+1}-\bm{w}_{t}). (1) This approximation yields the well-known descent lemma for gradient descent, which guarantees a decrease in loss when the LR η \eta satisfies η < 2 / λ max \eta<2/\lambda_{\max} . Here, λ max \lambda_{\max} is the maximum eigenvalue of the Hessian, which serves as a measure of the local curvature of the loss function. A standard analysis pipeline in optimization theory then proceeds by bounding quantities that appear in the lemma and deriving guarantees on the loss convergence. However, in deep learning, the quadratic approximation often fails to accurately capture the true training dynamics. Notably, Cohen et al. (2021) show that full-batch gradient descent (GD) typically operates at the Edge of Stability (EoS) when training neural networks. For a fixed LR η \eta , the maximum Hessian eigenvalue λ max \lambda_{\max} tends to increase during training and eventually oscillates around 2 / η 2/\eta , thus η ≈ 2 / λ max \eta\approx 2/\lambda_{\max} . Under the quadratic approximation, this places the dynamics exactly at the stability boundary of gradient descent, since the quadratic model predicts loss divergence once η > 2 / λ max \eta>2/\lambda_{\max} . Consequently, the descent lemma can no longer guarantee a persistent decrease of the loss. Yet in practice, the loss continues to decrease over long time scales. Similar EoS behavior has also been observed for full-batch adaptive optimizers such as Adam and RMSProp ( Cohen et al., 2022 ) , when curvature is measured using an appropriately preconditioned Hessian. (a) Illustration of Edge of Convexity (EoC). (b) Illustration of Edge of Stability (EoS). Figure 1: LLM pretraining on FineWeb-10B exhibits two distinct failure modes of the quadratic approximation. (a) EoC phenomenon : regardless of the LR choice, the training dynamics under quadratic approximation diverge due to persistent negative curvature, while the true dynamics remain stable. (b) EoS phenomenon : after compensating for negative curvature, the quadratic loss remains as stable as the true loss for 0.8 × 0.8\times and 1.0 × 1.0\times the training LR, but increasing the LR slightly to 1.2 × 1.2\times causes the quadratic loss to diverge. This shows that the current training LR is close to a critical stability threshold. See Sections 5.1 and 5.2 for details. The EoS phenomenon therefore exposes a fundamental limitation of existing optimization analyses for deep learning, as many such analyses critically rely on the descent lemma and the underlying quadratic approximation. This discrepancy has motivated a line of work that seeks to develop tools to understand training dynamics without critically relying on the quadratic approximation ( Arora et al., 2022 ; Damian et al., 2022 ; Cohen et al., 2024 ) . Despite these advances, existing empirical observations and theoretical analyses remain limited in several important aspects: (i) Most theoretical definitions of EoS focus on full-batch training, whereas stochastic training is more common in practice; (ii) Most studies focus on failures of the quadratic approximation caused by large positive Hessian eigenvalues, even though negative Hessian eigenvalues can also induce a similar gap between theory and practice, as we will elaborate in this work; (iii) Due to the prohibitive computational cost of computing and analyzing the Hessian, direct measurements of EoS are largely limited to relatively small-scale settings such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, leaving open whether the same failure mode persists in large-scale training.

sections.heading: Our Contributions.
sections.text: We present a systematic study of the failure modes of the quadratic approximation in stochastic, adaptive, and large-scale training, with a particular focus on LLM pretraining. • We first highlight an LR-independent failure mode of the quadratic approximation, where persistent negative curvature during training causes the quadratic dynamics to diverge regardless of the LR, even though the real dynamics remain stable. We term this phenomenon the Edge of Convexity (EoC). See Section 5.1 . • We isolate and remove the effect of EoC, and then study the Edge of Stability (EoS) as an LR-dependent failure mode. We propose a generalized definition of EoS for stochastic training with adaptive optimizers, based on whether increasing the LR induces significant divergence in the quadratic dynamics while leaving the real dynamics largely unchanged. For full-batch GD, our definition recovers the original EoS definition. See Sections 5.2 and 5.3 . • We design efficient methods to detect both EoC and EoS at scale with theoretical guarantees ( Sections A.2 and A.3 ). Our results on LLM pretraining suggest that (1) EoC consistently arises; (2) EoS is prevalent but not universal, and disappears when the LR becomes sufficiently small (e.g., after decay) or when the batch size falls below a critical threshold that scales linearly with the critical batch size ( Sections 6.2 , 6.3 and 6.4 ). (a) GPT-small (104M). (b) GPT-medium (344M). (c) GPT-large (787M). Figure 2: EoS and EoC appear across model sizes. At most checkpoints, the bottom heatmaps show a sharp transition from bounded displacement to explosion near LR factor 1.0 1.0 , indicating that the training LR is at the critical threshold of EoS. In the middle row, − λ min -\lambda_{\min} has a smaller magnitude than λ max \lambda_{\max} , corresponding to saddleness below the 0.1 0.1 reference line in the top plots and consistent with EoC. Each heatmap column is a checkpoint, and the vertical axis gives the simulated LR divided by the training LR. See Section 6.2 for the results and Section B.1 for training and detection settings.

sections.heading: Edge of Stability.
sections.text: Early studies connected sharpness and stability to optimizer behavior in neural network training: Wu et al. (2018) analyzed SGD minima selection through dynamical stability using sharpness and non-uniformity, and Xing et al. (2018) observed SGD “bouncing” between valley walls during training. Jastrzębski et al. (2018) then showed that SGD visits increasingly sharp regions up to a maximum set by LR and batch size, and that the step is often too large along the sharpest directions. Cohen et al. (2021) later demonstrated that full-batch gradient descent typically operates at an Edge of Stability (EoS), where the largest Hessian eigenvalue oscillates near 2 / η 2/\eta while loss decreases non-monotonically. Cohen et al. (2022) extended this phenomenon to adaptive methods via saturation of a preconditioned stability threshold. Finally, Arora et al. (2022) ; Li et al. (2022) ; Damian et al. (2022) ; Lyu et al. (2022) provide theoretical explanations for EoS in different training regimes, but a unified understanding of this phenomenon is still lacking.

sections.heading: Training Stability of Neural Networks
sections.text: Series works studied the training stability of constant LR SGD in quadratic losses via a linear system analysis of the second moment of the parameters ( Wu et al., 2018 ; Ma & Ying, 2021 ; Granziol et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Mulayoff & Michaeli, 2024 ) . They obtained tight conditions in the form of ‖ 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( 𝑰 − η ​ 𝑯 t ) ⊗ 2 ] ‖ ≤ 1 \|\mathbb{E}[({\bm{I}}-\eta{\bm{H}}_{t})^{\otimes 2}]\|\leq 1 , which are valid instability criteria for a particular Lyapunov function. However, in the training neural networks with (S)GD, the unstable convergence phenomenon was observed ( Wu et al., 2018 ; Xing et al., 2018 ; Jastrzębski et al., 2018 ) , formally identified and termed Edge of Stability (EoS) ( Cohen et al., 2021 ) . Subsequently, several studies sought to explain this unstable convergence ( Ma et al., 2022 ; Ahn et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Arora et al., 2022 ; Damian et al., 2022 ; Cohen et al., 2024 ) . Among them, Cohen et al. (2024) gave a general characterization of the oscillatory dynamics of deep learning in the EoS regime via a time-averaged differential equation termed central flow . However, the effectiveness of the quadratic approximation was never carefully studied in the large-scale neural network training, hence it is not clear when and how the quadratic approximation fails or not in the realistic regime.

sections.heading: Hessian Spectrum of Neural Networks.
sections.text: Most studies on the Hessian spectrum of neural networks reported that the Hessian spectra of neural networks consist of a “bulk” together with a few large “outliers” in magnitude ( LeCun et al., 2002 ; Dauphin et al., 2014 ; Sagun et al., 2016 ; Sagun et al., 2017 ; Ghorbani et al., 2019 ; Chaudhari et al., 2019 ; Yao et al., 2020 ) . Among them, Sagun et al. (2016) ; Sagun et al. (2017) mentioned that there are still negative eigenvalues during training, but their magnitude is much smaller than the large outliers. More recent works reported and explained a near-block diagonal structure in the Hessian spectrum of CNNs and Transformers ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) . However, one thing that has long been overlooked is the characterization of the negative eigenvalues in the population Hessian during large-scale training. In this work, we present detailed empirical findings of the negative eigenvalues across different setups in large-scale neural network training.

sections.heading: Comparison with Andreyev & Beneventano (2024) .
sections.text: The recent work ( Andreyev & Beneventano, 2024 ) is among the most relevant to this work, which defines Edge of Stochastic Stability for SGD via the batch sharpness, where Batch Sharpness hovers around 2 / η 2/\eta . Compared to Andreyev & Beneventano (2024) , our work (1) In the full-batch setting, our definition for EoS can be reduced to the original definition of EoS by Cohen et al. (2021) ; Cohen et al. (2022) , while theirs cannot; (2) We also identify another failure mode of the quadratic approximation called Edge of Convexity (EoC); (3) We provide scalable EoS and EoC detection methods with theoretical guarantees; (4) We conduct experiments on large-scale LLM pretraining with AdamW, while most of their experiments are limited to ResNets on CIFAR-10 and SVHN with vanilla SGD.

sections.heading: 4 Stability of Stochastic Gradient Descent on Quadratics
sections.text: The full-batch EoS reviewed above is insightful but incomplete for modern neural networks since it relies on two simplifying conditions. First, the Hessian is assumed to be positive semidefinite. If it has a negative eigenvalue, then the local quadratic dynamics contain an exploding direction for every positive LR, so the usual positive curvature stability threshold is no longer the only source of instability. Second, the analysis is deterministic and applies to full-batch gradient descent. It does not capture the additional randomness introduced by mini-batch sampling. sections.heading: 4.2 Positive Curvature Divergence and Critical LR
sections.text: Next, we show that even if we factor out those directions causing negative divergence and focus on the locally convex subspace, the instability can also arise from mini-batch noise and admits a critical LR threshold. The most direct construction is to keep only the directions of positive curvature, discarding the eigenvectors of 𝑨 {\bm{A}} with nonpositive eigenvalues. On the remaining subspace the population quadratic is strongly convex. Let Π + \Pi^{+} be the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace of 𝑨 {\bm{A}} with positive eigenvalues. sections.heading: Negative curvature makes the quadratic model unstable.

sections.heading: Measuring population negative curvature during LLM pretraining.
sections.text: Early studies on small image and synthetic datasets reported negative Hessian eigenvalues much smaller in magnitude than the largest positive eigenvalue ( Sagun et al., 2016 ; Sagun et al., 2017 ; Alain et al., 2019 ) . In this paper, we extend these measurements to the population Hessian throughout LLM pretraining ( Figure 2 ). Doing so requires λ min ​ ( 𝑯 t 0 ) \lambda_{\min}({\bm{H}}_{t_{0}}) . The usual approach at scale is to run Lanczos on one mini-batch Hessian ( Ghorbani et al., 2019 ; Yao et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . This gives λ min ​ ( 𝑯 ℬ ) \lambda_{\min}({\bm{H}}_{\mathcal{B}}) . And since λ min ​ ( ⋅ ) \lambda_{\min}(\cdot) is concave, Jensen’s inequality gives 𝔼 ⁡ [ λ min ​ ( 𝑯 ℬ ) ] ≤ λ min ​ ( 𝑯 t 0 ) \mathbb{E}[\lambda_{\min}({\bm{H}}_{\mathcal{B}})]\leq\lambda_{\min}({\bm{H}}_{t_{0}}) , so the mini-batch value is biased below the population value. This downward bias can be substantial in practice. To this end, we propose a stochastic power iteration for the estimate of λ min ​ ( 𝑯 t 0 ) \lambda_{\min}({\bm{H}}_{t_{0}}) , which further gives the systematic detection of EoC. The complete EoC detection procedure is given in Section A.2 , along with the theoretical guarantee in Section C.3 .

sections.heading: 5.2 Edge of Stability under Stochastic Training
sections.text: Even after removing the effect of EoC (i.e., restricting to the positive-curvature subspace in Definition 4.3 ), the quadratic approximation can still diverge. This divergence is caused by positive curvature when the LR exceeds the critical threshold η ⋆ ​ ( 𝒘 t 0 ) \eta_{\star}(\bm{w}_{t_{0}}) . More subtly, neural network training often operates near this boundary: a tiny positive increase in the LR can already trigger divergence. Stochastic Edge of Stability (EoS) at w t 0 \bm{w}_{t_{0}} . Training is at EoS when the current LR is close to the stochastic critical LR on the positive-curvature subspace, η ≈ η ⋆ ​ ( 𝒘 t 0 ) . \eta\approx\eta_{\star}(\bm{w}_{t_{0}}). The mean curvature is positive definite on this subspace, so the LRs with bounded second moments have a single critical endpoint ( Section C.2 ). In the full-batch case at a stationary point, this critical LR is 2 / λ max ​ ( 𝑯 t 0 ) 2/\lambda_{\max}({\bm{H}}_{t_{0}}) whenever λ max ​ ( 𝑯 t 0 ) > 0 \lambda_{\max}({\bm{H}}_{t_{0}})>0 , as computed after Definition 4.3 , which recovers the full-batch EoS condition of Cohen et al. (2021) . See Section 2 for comparison with previous work on stochastic EoS. As discussed in Section 4 , for the stochastic case, even after projection, mean-square stability is governed by the second-moment operator 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝑴 t + ⊗ 𝑴 t + ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝑴 t + ] ⊗ 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝑴 t + ] + Cov ⁡ ( 𝑴 t + ) . \mathbb{E}[{\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}\otimes{\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}]=\mathbb{E}[{\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}]\otimes\mathbb{E}[{\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}]+\mathrm{Cov}({\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}). The covariance term can shift the critical LR away from 2 / λ max 2/\lambda_{\max} . Moreover, directly solving ρ ⁡ ( 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝑴 t + ⊗ 𝑴 t + ] ) < 1 \rho\!\left(\mathbb{E}[{\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}\otimes{\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}]\right)<1 is infeasible at neural network scale, since 𝑴 t + ⊗ 𝑴 t + {\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}\otimes{\bm{M}}_{t}^{+} is a fourth-order object and its entries are affected by noisy mini-batch Hessian samples. Thus, the definitions above reveal two practical obstacles. First, EoC and EoS live on different curvature subspaces, but explicitly separating these subspaces is infeasible for large NNs, especially for LLM pretraining. Second, the stochastic EoS threshold is not only determined by λ max \lambda_{\max} alone but also correlated with the stochastic noise in training, so we cannot detect it by simply checking whether η ​ λ max ≈ 2 \eta\lambda_{\max}\approx 2 .

sections.heading: EoS detection.
sections.text: We use a local simulation to detect EoS in pretraining. First, to compensate for negative curvature, we add λ 𝖯 2 ​ ‖ 𝒘 − 𝒘 t 0 ‖ 2 \tfrac{\lambda_{\mathsf{P}}}{2}\|\bm{w}-\bm{w}_{t_{0}}\|^{2} to the local quadratic surrogate ( 10 ), with λ 𝖯 = max ⁡ { 0 , − λ ^ min } \lambda_{\mathsf{P}}=\max\{0,-\widehat{\lambda}_{\min}\} , where λ ^ min \widehat{\lambda}_{\min} is the estimate of the minimum eigenvalue from Section A.2 . We then simulate SGD on this loss from the checkpoint for a fixed number of steps over a grid of LRs around the training LR η \eta , using the same batch sequence for every run. The estimate η ^ ⋆ \widehat{\eta}_{\star} is the smallest LR in the grid for which the displacement norm ‖ 𝒘 − 𝒘 t 0 ‖ \|{\bm{w}}-{\bm{w}}_{t_{0}}\| reaches a prescribed cutoff. We declare EoS when η ^ ⋆ \widehat{\eta}_{\star} is close to η \eta . The complete procedure is given in Section A.3 and theoretical analysis is in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Illustration on CIFAR-10.
sections.text: Figure 7 applies both detectors to ResNet-20 and ResNet-32 trained with SGD. Each column is a checkpoint, each row an LR factor, and color encodes the final displacement norm of the local simulation. Across most checkpoints in the middle phase of training, the bounded-to-exploding boundary lies at LR factor 1.0 1.0 (white dashed line). The training LR is close to η ⋆ \eta_{\star} , and SGD training operates at the EoS for a large part of training. Section 6 applies the same protocol to LLM pretraining with AdamW, with definitions and detectors extended to adaptive methods below.

sections.heading: 5.3 Adaptive Gradient Methods at the Edge of Convexity and Edge of Stability
sections.text: So far, the discussion has focused on SGD. Modern LLMs are usually trained with adaptive methods such as AdamW ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017 ) . The effective curvature and its saddleness are 𝑨 ≔ 𝑷 − 1 / 2 𝑯 t 0 𝑷 − 1 / 2 + λ WD 𝑰 , ν ≔ max { 0 , − μ ¯ min } / μ ¯ max , {\bm{A}}\coloneqq{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}{\bm{H}}_{t_{0}}{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}+\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}{\bm{I}},\nu\coloneqq\max\{0,-\bar{\mu}_{\min}\}/\bar{\mu}_{\max}, where μ ¯ min = λ min ​ ( 𝑨 ) \bar{\mu}_{\min}=\lambda_{\min}({\bm{A}}) and μ ¯ max = λ max ​ ( 𝑨 ) > 0 \bar{\mu}_{\max}=\lambda_{\max}({\bm{A}})>0 . sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: We apply our detection methods to study EoS and EoC during language model pretraining. Our experiments examine how broadly these phenomena occur and how EoS depends on the training configurations like batch size and learning rate schedule. (a) Cosine schedule. (b) Multistep schedule I. (c) Multistep schedule II. Figure 3: Training may leave the EoS regime after LR decay. In (a) and (b), the transition from bounded displacement to explosion moves to larger LR factors during cosine decay and after the abrupt multistep LR drop, respectively. After the larger LR drop in (c), the local simulations remain bounded at the training LR for the rest of the observed run, where training enters the stable regime and does not come back to EoS. See Sections 6.4 , B.4 and B.5 for further discussion. (a) EoS batch size threshold vs. critical batch size. (b) Critical LR factor q q vs. batch size. sections.heading: 6.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We pretrain GPT-style models at four scales ranging from 43M to 787M. Unless otherwise specified, runs use FineWeb ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) , AdamW ( WD = 0.1 \mathrm{WD}=0.1 , β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 ), sequence length 1024, and a Warm–Stable–Decay (WSD) LR schedule ( Hu et al., 2024 ) with 4% warmup steps and 20% decay steps. Full details are provided in Appendix B .

sections.heading: 6.2 EoS and EoC Are Widely Observed
sections.text: We evaluate EoS and EoC at over 3,000 3{,}000 checkpoints from more than 100 100 pretraining runs spanning different model sizes, peak LRs, batch sizes, and shapes of LR schedules. Both phenomena are widely observed across our experiments ( Figures 2 , 5 , 8 , 9 and 3 ). At many checkpoints, the estimated critical LR is close to the training LR, while the estimated minimum eigenvalue is negative and saddleness is below 0.1 0.1 , consistent with EoS and EoC, respectively. Additional results and discussion are given in Sections B.2 , B.3 , B.4 and B.5 . We next examine how these phenomena depend on the training configuration. Specifically, we focus on two key training hyperparameters: batch size and the LR schedule. Note that EoC remains widely observed as these hyperparameters vary, so the following analysis focuses primarily on how they affect EoS. (a) Mean critical LR factor. (b) Final eval loss. Figure 5: Training may go beyond EoS and enter an extremely unstable regime with large LR. (a) As the peak LR increases, the critical LR factor q = η ^ ⋆ / η q=\widehat{\eta}_{\star}/\eta , averaged over the tested checkpoints, falls from near the reference line at 1.0 1.0 to well below it. Values near 1.0 1.0 indicate EoS, while smaller values mean that the training LR exceeds the estimated critical LR. (b) These large peak LRs also yield higher final evaluation loss. See Sections 6.2 and 6.4 for further discussion.

sections.heading: 6.3 Batch size dependence of EoS
sections.text: For the dependence of batch size, we first show that EoS emerges above a threshold of batch size, which is referred to as the EoS Batch Size (EBZ) . We then demonstrate an interesting correlation between EBZ and the critical batch size (CBZ) across different datasets.

sections.heading: EoS emerges above the EBZ threshold.
sections.text: Figure 9 shows that EoS is observed over a larger fraction of training at B = 512 B=512 and B = 1024 B=1024 than at B = 256 B=256 . For the two larger batch sizes, the transition from bounded displacement to explosion stays near LR factor 1.0 1.0 over much of the stable phase, indicating that the training LR is close to the estimated critical LR. Below this batch size threshold, the compensated local simulations at checkpoints after the early phase of training remain bounded at every tested LR factor. These runs use GPT-extra-small on FineWeb with WSD schedules and adjust the LR, weight decay, and β 2 \beta_{2} according to the batch size scaling rule in Section B.3 . Further, across all five datasets, Figure 4(b) shows that the critical LR factor, averaged over the tested checkpoints of each run, decreases as batch size increases. We estimate EBZ as the batch size at which the fitted mean critical LR factor first decreases to 1.1 1.1 as batch size increases. This corresponds to the crossing at 1.1 1.1 marked in the figure.

sections.heading: EBZ and CBZ show a positive correlation across datasets.
sections.text: In Figure 4(a) , each point represents one dataset, and the points follow an overall upward linear trend. FineWeb has the largest EBZ and CBZ, while OpenWebMath has the smallest values of both. Here, CBZ is estimated from the same training runs as EBZ and denotes the largest batch size whose final evaluation loss is within 0.3 % 0.3\% of the best loss in that dataset’s sweep. Thus, datasets with a larger threshold for EoS also tend to maintain near optimal final evaluation loss at larger batch sizes. Full sweep and estimation details are given in Section B.3 .

sections.heading: 6.4 LR Dependence of EoS
sections.text: We next show that LR decay can cause training to leave EoS, and that training may not return to the EoS regime after a sufficiently large LR decay. We also show that training at excessively large peak LRs can enter an extremely unstable regime beyond EoS.

sections.heading: Training can enter the stable regime after LR decay.
sections.text: Before LR decay, training often operates at EoS, with the training LR close to the estimated critical LR ( Figures 3 , 11 and 12 ). After the abrupt LR drop in Figure 3(b) , the transition from bounded displacement to explosion moves to larger LR factors. The estimated critical LR is now higher than the reduced training LR, and the compensated local simulation stays bounded at the training LR over the tested horizon. As training continues, the estimated critical LR can fall back toward the current training LR and EoS can return, as in Figure 11(d) . With a sufficiently large LR reduction, however, the estimated critical LR stays well above the training LR for the rest of the observed run ( Figures 3(c) , 11(c) and 12(d) ). The compensated local simulations then remain bounded at the training LR, and EoS does not return. The effects of the drop magnitude and decay duration are discussed in Sections B.4 and B.5 .

sections.heading: Training can enter an extremely unstable regime with large LR.
sections.text: Training with peak LRs substantially above the empirically optimal range can yield higher loss and enter an extremely unstable regime beyond EoS ( Figure 5 ). In this regime, the compensated local quadratic dynamics still allow a critical LR, but it lies far below the training LR. For example, at peak LR 0.04 0.04 , the estimated critical LR is only about one tenth of the training LR on average, and the compensated local simulations explode at the training LR. See Section B.2 for further discussion and Figures 14 , 15 and 16 for detailed diagnostics across model sizes and peak LRs.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper extends the definition of EoS to the LLM training under a unified framework, together with another clearly clarified phenomenon EoC, accounting for the two failure modes of the quadratic approximation. Several directions remain open for future study. (i) Our experiments mainly focus on SGD and AdamW. It is interesting to see how EoS would behave when training with other optimizers like Muon. (ii) Fully understanding EoS and EoC also calls for solid theoretical analyses of the realistic neural network training dynamics.

sections.heading: Appendix A Detecting EoC and EoS for Adaptive Gradient Methods
sections.text: Here we provide detailed detection methods of EoC and EoS for AGMs. We first define the local AGM model, its saddleness, and its critical LR in Section A.1 . Sections A.2 and A.3 then describe the EoC and EoS detection procedures and their guarantees. Both procedures use Hessian-vector products without forming the Hessian. Section A.4 gives their computational cost. The complete theoretical statements and proofs are in Appendices C , D , E and F .

sections.heading: A.1 Adaptive Gradient Methods
sections.text: We consider adaptive gradient methods (AGMs) with a momentum vector 𝒎 t {\bm{m}}_{t} and a positive definite preconditioner 𝑷 t {\bm{P}}_{t} . For the mini-batch loss ℒ ℬ t \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}} , the updates are 𝒎 t + 1 \displaystyle{\bm{m}}_{t+1} = β 1 𝒎 t + ( 1 − β 1 ) ∇ ℒ ℬ t ( 𝒘 t ) , \displaystyle=\beta_{1}{\bm{m}}_{t}+(1-\beta_{1})\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}(\bm{w}_{t}), 𝑷 t + 1 \displaystyle{\bm{P}}_{t+1} = Ψ ⁡ ( 𝑷 t , ∇ ℒ ℬ t ​ ( 𝒘 t ) , 𝒘 t ) , \displaystyle=\Psi\bigl({\bm{P}}_{t},\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}(\bm{w}_{t}),\bm{w}_{t}\bigr), 𝒘 t + 1 \displaystyle\bm{w}_{t+1} = 𝒘 t − η ​ 𝑷 t + 1 − 1 ​ 𝒎 t + 1 − η ​ λ WD ​ 𝒘 t . \displaystyle=\bm{w}_{t}-\eta{\bm{P}}_{t+1}^{-1}{\bm{m}}_{t+1}-\eta\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}\bm{w}_{t}. Here η > 0 \eta>0 is the LR, 0 ≤ β 1 < 1 0\leq\beta_{1}<1 is the momentum coefficient, and λ WD ≥ 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}\geq 0 is the decoupled weight decay coefficient. The preconditioner update Ψ \Psi preserves positive definiteness.

sections.text: Fix a checkpoint 𝒘 t 0 \bm{w}_{t_{0}} . For each mini-batch ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} , we approximate its loss ℒ ℬ t \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}} by the second-order Taylor expansion around this checkpoint. Write ϵ = 𝒘 − 𝒘 t 0 \bm{\epsilon}=\bm{w}-\bm{w}_{t_{0}} for the displacement, and define the gradient and Hessian at the checkpoint by 𝒈 ℬ t ≔ ∇ ℒ ℬ t ​ ( 𝒘 t 0 ) , 𝑯 ℬ t ≔ ∇ 2 ℒ ℬ t ​ ( 𝒘 t 0 ) . {\bm{g}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}\coloneqq\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}(\bm{w}_{t_{0}}),\qquad{\bm{H}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}\coloneqq\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}(\bm{w}_{t_{0}}). The resulting quadratic surrogate is Q ℬ t ​ ( 𝒘 t 0 + ϵ ) ≔ ℒ ℬ t ​ ( 𝒘 t 0 ) + 𝒈 ℬ t ⊤ ​ ϵ + 1 2 ​ ϵ ⊤ ​ 𝑯 ℬ t ​ ϵ . (13) This surrogate matches the loss, gradient, and Hessian at the checkpoint and omits terms of higher order in the displacement. At each local step, we sample a fresh batch and use its surrogate in place of the neural network loss. The coefficients 𝒈 ℬ t {\bm{g}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}} and 𝑯 ℬ t {\bm{H}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}} are always evaluated at 𝒘 t 0 \bm{w}_{t_{0}} .

sections.text: We freeze the preconditioner at 𝑷 ≔ 𝑷 t 0 ≻ 0 {\bm{P}}\coloneqq{\bm{P}}_{t_{0}}\succ 0 and let the momentum evolve under the surrogate gradients. Let ϵ t \bm{\epsilon}_{t} be the displacement after t t local steps. The surrogate gradient at this displacement is 𝒈 ℬ t + 𝑯 ℬ t ​ ϵ t {\bm{g}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}+{\bm{H}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}\bm{\epsilon}_{t} . Keeping η \eta , β 1 \beta_{1} and λ WD \lambda_{\mathrm{WD}} fixed, the local updates become 𝒎 t + 1 \displaystyle{\bm{m}}_{t+1} = β 1 ​ 𝒎 t + ( 1 − β 1 ) ​ ( 𝒈 ℬ t + 𝑯 ℬ t ​ ϵ t ) , \displaystyle=\beta_{1}{\bm{m}}_{t}+(1-\beta_{1})({\bm{g}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}+{\bm{H}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}\bm{\epsilon}_{t}), (14) ϵ t + 1 \displaystyle\bm{\epsilon}_{t+1} = ϵ t − η ​ 𝑷 − 1 ​ 𝒎 t + 1 − η ​ λ WD ​ ( 𝒘 t 0 + ϵ t ) . \displaystyle=\bm{\epsilon}_{t}-\eta{\bm{P}}^{-1}{\bm{m}}_{t+1}-\eta\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}(\bm{w}_{t_{0}}+\bm{\epsilon}_{t}). In preconditioned coordinates, we stack the momentum and displacement as 𝒛 t ≔ ( η 𝑷 − 1 / 2 𝒎 t , 𝑷 1 / 2 ϵ t ) ⊤ . {\bm{z}}_{t}\coloneqq(\eta{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}{\bm{m}}_{t},{\bm{P}}^{1/2}\bm{\epsilon}_{t})^{\top}. Then ( 14 ) has the affine form 𝒛 t + 1 = 𝑴 t ​ ( η ) ​ 𝒛 t + 𝒒 t . {\bm{z}}_{t+1}={\bm{M}}_{t}(\eta){\bm{z}}_{t}+{\bm{q}}_{t}. (15) Write 𝑫 ℬ t = 𝑷 − 1 / 2 𝑯 ℬ t 𝑷 − 1 / 2 {\bm{D}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}={\bm{P}}^{-1/2}{\bm{H}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}{\bm{P}}^{-1/2} for the preconditioned mini-batch Hessian. The transition matrix and forcing are 𝑴 t ​ ( η ) \displaystyle{\bm{M}}_{t}(\eta) = [ β 1 ​ 𝑰 ( 1 − β 1 ) ​ η ​ 𝑫 ℬ t − β 1 ​ 𝑰 ( 1 − η ​ λ WD ) ​ 𝑰 − ( 1 − β 1 ) ​ η ​ 𝑫 ℬ t ] , \displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}\beta_{1}{\bm{I}}&(1-\beta_{1})\eta{\bm{D}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}\\ -\beta_{1}{\bm{I}}&(1-\eta\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}){\bm{I}}-(1-\beta_{1})\eta{\bm{D}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}\end{bmatrix}, 𝒒 t \displaystyle{\bm{q}}_{t} = [ ( 1 − β 1 ) η 𝑷 − 1 / 2 𝒈 ℬ t − ( 1 − β 1 ) η 𝑷 − 1 / 2 𝒈 ℬ t − η λ WD 𝑷 1 / 2 𝒘 t 0 ] . \displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}(1-\beta_{1})\eta{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}{\bm{g}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}\\ -(1-\beta_{1})\eta{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}{\bm{g}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}-\eta\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}{\bm{P}}^{1/2}\bm{w}_{t_{0}}\end{bmatrix}. Two trajectories driven by the same batches have the same forcing 𝒒 t {\bm{q}}_{t} . Their difference therefore evolves by multiplication with 𝑴 t ​ ( η ) {\bm{M}}_{t}(\eta) . We use this homogeneous evolution to define stability of local perturbations.

sections.heading: Effective curvature and saddleness.
sections.text: Let 𝑯 t 0 ≔ ∇ 2 ℒ ​ ( 𝒘 t 0 ) {\bm{H}}_{t_{0}}\coloneqq\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}(\bm{w}_{t_{0}}) be the population Hessian. The preconditioned Hessians and effective curvatures are 𝑫 t 0 \displaystyle{\bm{D}}_{t_{0}} ≔ 𝑷 − 1 / 2 𝑯 t 0 𝑷 − 1 / 2 , \displaystyle\coloneqq{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}{\bm{H}}_{t_{0}}{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}, 𝑨 \displaystyle{\bm{A}} ≔ 𝑫 t 0 + λ WD ​ 𝑰 , \displaystyle\coloneqq{\bm{D}}_{t_{0}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}{\bm{I}}, (16) 𝑫 ℬ t \displaystyle{\bm{D}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}} ≔ 𝑷 − 1 / 2 𝑯 ℬ t 𝑷 − 1 / 2 , \displaystyle\coloneqq{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}{\bm{H}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}, 𝑨 ℬ t \displaystyle{\bm{A}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}} ≔ 𝑫 ℬ t + λ WD ​ 𝑰 . \displaystyle\coloneqq{\bm{D}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}{\bm{I}}. If λ min ​ ( 𝑨 ) < 0 \lambda_{\min}({\bm{A}})<0 , some local perturbations grow in mean at every positive LR, even with momentum ( Lemma C.5 ). We measure the size of this negative effective curvature relative to the largest positive effective curvature. Definition A.1 (Saddleness for AGMs) . Suppose λ max ​ ( 𝑨 ) > 0 \lambda_{\max}({\bm{A}})>0 . The AGM saddleness at the checkpoint is ν ≔ max ⁡ { 0 , − λ min ​ ( 𝑨 ) } λ max ​ ( 𝑨 ) . \nu\coloneqq\frac{\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}({\bm{A}})\}}{\lambda_{\max}({\bm{A}})}. (17) The preconditioner and weight decay are included through 𝑨 {\bm{A}} . AGM training is at EoC when λ min ​ ( 𝑨 ) < 0 \lambda_{\min}({\bm{A}})<0 and this ratio is small. For SGD without weight decay, 𝑨 = 𝑯 t 0 {\bm{A}}={\bm{H}}_{t_{0}} , so this definition reduces to Definition 5.1 .

sections.heading: Critical LR.
sections.text: To isolate instability caused by the LR, we remove the directions of nonpositive effective curvature. Let Π + \Pi^{+} project onto the strictly positive eigenspace of 𝑨 {\bm{A}} , assumed to be nonempty. We project both momentum and displacement in preconditioned coordinates at every update. The effective curvature after the projection is therefore positive definite on this subspace. Write 𝑴 t + ​ ( η ) {\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}(\eta) and 𝒒 t + {\bm{q}}_{t}^{+} for the transition and forcing in coordinates on this subspace. The projected local system is 𝒛 t + 1 + = 𝑴 t + ​ ( η ) ​ 𝒛 t + + 𝒒 t + . {\bm{z}}_{t+1}^{+}={\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}(\eta){\bm{z}}_{t}^{+}+{\bm{q}}_{t}^{+}. (18) Following Definition 4.1 , we call this system mean-square stable if sup t ≥ 0 𝔼 ​ ‖ 𝒛 t + ‖ 2 < ∞ for every deterministic initial state ​ 𝒛 0 + . \sup_{t\geq 0}\mathbb{E}\|{\bm{z}}_{t}^{+}\|^{2}<\infty\qquad\text{for every deterministic initial state }{\bm{z}}_{0}^{+}. The initial state includes both momentum and displacement. This definition allows persistent fluctuations and does not require the second moment to tend to zero. Definition A.2 (Critical LR for AGMs) . Keep the checkpoint, 𝑷 {\bm{P}} , β 1 \beta_{1} , λ WD \lambda_{\mathrm{WD}} , and the batch distribution fixed as the LR varies. The AGM critical LR is η ⋆ ≔ sup { η > 0 : the projected system ( 18 ) is mean-square stable } . \eta_{\star}\coloneqq\sup\bigl\{\eta>0:\text{the projected system \eqref{eq:agm-projected-local-system} is mean-square stable}\bigr\}. (19) The next proposition gives an equivalent way to determine this critical LR from the homogeneous transition. Its second-moment matrix is 𝑲 + ​ ( η ) ≔ 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝑴 t + ​ ( η ) ⊗ 𝑴 t + ​ ( η ) ] . {\bm{K}}^{+}(\eta)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[{\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}(\eta)\otimes{\bm{M}}_{t}^{+}(\eta)]. (20) We assume that the pairs ( 𝑯 ℬ t , 𝒈 ℬ t ) ({\bm{H}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}},{\bm{g}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}) are i.i.d. and independent of the initial state. Both entries have finite second moments, each Hessian is symmetric, and their means are the population derivatives at the checkpoint. These are the mini-batch assumptions of Assumption C.1 . Proposition A.3 (Spectral characterization of the AGM critical LR) . Under Assumption C.1 , fix 𝐏 ≻ 0 {\bm{P}}\succ 0 , 0 ≤ β 1 < 1 0\leq\beta_{1}<1 and λ WD ≥ 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}\geq 0 . Suppose the strictly positive eigenspace of 𝐀 {\bm{A}} is nonempty. The critical LR in Definition A.2 satisfies 0 < η ⋆ = sup { η > 0 : ρ ⁡ ( 𝑲 + ​ ( η ) ) < 1 } < ∞ . 0<\eta_{\star}=\sup\bigl\{\eta>0:\rho({\bm{K}}^{+}(\eta))<1\bigr\}<\infty. (21) Moreover, ρ ⁡ ( 𝑲 + ​ ( η ) ) ​ { < 1 , 0 < η < η ⋆ , = 1 , η = η ⋆ , > 1 , η > η ⋆ . \rho\bigl({\bm{K}}^{+}(\eta)\bigr)\begin{cases}<1,&0<\eta<\eta_{\star},\\ =1,&\eta=\eta_{\star},\\ >1,&\eta>\eta_{\star}.\end{cases} (22) Below η ⋆ \eta_{\star} , the projected affine system is mean-square stable. Above η ⋆ \eta_{\star} , some deterministic initialization has an unbounded second moment. At η ⋆ \eta_{\star} , boundedness can depend on the forcing. Thus the proposition equates the two critical LRs without identifying boundedness with strict decay at the boundary. The proof is in Section D.6 . AGM training is at EoS when its training LR is close to η ⋆ \eta_{\star} . The stability notion and the projection are those of the main text. For SGD without weight decay, this critical LR is the one of Definition 4.3 applied to the local quadratic. The next two subsections describe how we estimate the effective curvature and the critical LR of this local model.

sections.heading: A.2 EoC Detection
sections.text: EoC at 𝒘 t 0 \bm{w}_{t_{0}} means that 𝑨 {\bm{A}} has a negative eigenvalue while the saddleness ν \nu is small. Detecting it requires λ max ​ ( 𝑨 ) \lambda_{\max}({\bm{A}}) and λ min ​ ( 𝑨 ) \lambda_{\min}({\bm{A}}) . We estimate the maximum eigenvalue by Lanczos on a large batch. In our measurements, the top eigenpair varies little across mini-batches, whereas the bottom eigenvectors are nearly orthogonal ( Figure 6 ). Lanczos on one mini-batch estimates λ min ​ ( 𝑨 ℬ t ) \lambda_{\min}({\bm{A}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}) , whose expectation is at most λ min ​ ( 𝑨 ) \lambda_{\min}({\bm{A}}) by Jensen’s inequality. We therefore estimate λ min ​ ( 𝑨 ) \lambda_{\min}({\bm{A}}) by a stochastic power iteration method that draws a fresh mini-batch at every step. Figure 6: Mini-batch Lanczos estimates are stable for the top eigenpair but unstable for the bottom eigenpair. sections.heading: The expected detector.
sections.text: We analyze an idealized version, the expected detector. It runs the same stochastic dynamics but replaces the single trajectory by 𝔼 ​ ‖ ϵ t ‖ 2 \mathbb{E}\|\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\|^{2} , since η ⋆ \eta_{\star} is a mean-square threshold ( Section C.2 ). Fix a search window ℐ \mathcal{I} around η \eta , the horizon T T and a cutoff M > 1 M>1 . Run the same compensated dynamics from every unit displacement ‖ ϵ 0 ‖ = 1 \|\bm{\epsilon}_{0}\|=1 with the checkpoint momentum, and take the expectation over the mini-batches. The expected detector returns η ¯ ⋆ ​ ( M , T ) = sup { η ′ ∈ ℐ : max 0 ≤ t ≤ T ⁡ 𝔼 ​ ‖ ϵ t ‖ 2 ≤ M 2 ​ for every ​ ‖ ϵ 0 ‖ = 1 } . \bar{\eta}_{\star}(M,T)=\sup\Bigl\{\eta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{I}:\ \max_{0\leq t\leq T}\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\|^{2}\leq M^{2}\ \text{for every }\|\bm{\epsilon}_{0}\|=1\Bigr\}. The detector accepts η ′ \eta^{\prime} if the condition in the braces holds, so η ¯ ⋆ ​ ( M , T ) \bar{\eta}_{\star}(M,T) is the supremum of the accepted LRs ( Section C.4 ). We keep η ^ ⋆ \widehat{\eta}_{\star} for the output of the algorithm. The implemented detector differs from it in three ways. First, the expected detector takes the supremum of accepted LRs in a continuous window, while the algorithm returns the first exploding LR in an increasing grid. Finite-horizon acceptance need not be monotone in the LR, so these thresholds can differ. Second, the expected detector starts from unit displacements, so M > 1 M>1 is a relative cutoff, while the algorithm starts from zero and uses M M as an absolute bound on ‖ ϵ t ‖ 𝑷 \|\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\|_{{\bm{P}}} . Third, the expected detector takes the expectation of ‖ ϵ t ‖ 2 \|\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\|^{2} over the mini-batch sequence, while the algorithm runs one trajectory. The algorithm uses the preconditioner norm, in which the compensation is measured; the analysis of the expected detector is unchanged under this norm ( Remark F.10 ).

sections.heading: A.4 Cost of a Hessian-Vector Product
Matrix-multiplication count for a linear layer.
sections.text: Consider a linear layer 𝒀 = 𝑿 ​ 𝑾 , {\bm{Y}}={\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}, (24) where 𝑿 ∈ ℝ n × d in {\bm{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} holds a batch of n n inputs, 𝑾 ∈ ℝ d in × d out {\bm{W}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times d_{\mathrm{out}}} , and 𝒀 ∈ ℝ n × d out {\bm{Y}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{out}}} . Let 𝑮 = ∂ ℒ / ∂ 𝒀 {\bm{G}}=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial{\bm{Y}} be the upstream gradient. The forward pass uses one general matrix multiplication (GEMM), 𝒀 = 𝑿 ​ 𝑾 ⇒ 1 ​ GEMM . {\bm{Y}}={\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad 1~\text{GEMM}. (25) The first-order backward pass computes gradients with respect to 𝑿 {\bm{X}} and 𝑾 {\bm{W}} , ∂ ℒ ∂ 𝑿 = 𝑮 ​ 𝑾 ⊤ , ∂ ℒ ∂ 𝑾 = 𝑿 ⊤ ​ 𝑮 , \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial{\bm{X}}}={\bm{G}}{\bm{W}}^{\top},\qquad\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial{\bm{W}}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{G}}, (26) which costs two GEMMs. Thus, a forward and backward pass through a linear layer costs approximately three GEMMs, ignoring elementwise operations. The autograd procedure above computes an HVP by backpropagating through the gradient computation in a second reverse-mode pass. For layers whose cost is dominated by matrix multiplication, this incurs overhead comparable to an additional forward and backward pass through the same linear operators, plus extra GEMMs from differentiating the backward equations. Including the required second-order terms gives approximately 1 ⏟ forward + 2 ⏟ backward + 2 ⏟ differentiate backward (w.r.t. ​ 𝑾 ​ ) + 4 ⏟ propagate directional adjoints ≈ 9 ​ GEMMs . \underbrace{1}_{\text{forward}}\;+\;\underbrace{2}_{\text{backward}}\;+\;\underbrace{2}_{\text{differentiate backward (w.r.t.\ }{\bm{W}}\text{)}}\;+\;\underbrace{4}_{\text{propagate directional adjoints}}\;\approx\;9~\text{GEMMs}. (27) This is about 3 × 3\times the cost of one gradient evaluation ( 9 9 versus 3 3 GEMMs per linear layer), or 9 × 9\times a forward pass when GEMMs dominate. Since transformer blocks contain many such linear layers (QKV projections, the attention output projection, and the two MLP projections), this constant-factor overhead provides a practical estimate of HVP cost for our models.

sections.heading: Model architectures.
sections.text: Table 1 lists the models used in our experiments. Table 1: Model architectures used in our experiments. Model #Layers Hidden Dim #Heads Head Dim Params GPT-extra-small 4 768 12 64 43M GPT-small 12 768 12 64 104M GPT-medium 24 1,024 16 64 344M GPT-large 36 1,280 20 64 787M For each dataset, we train a byte-level BPE tokenizer with a vocabulary of 8,192 8{,}192 tokens and use it for all model sizes. We use a small vocabulary instead of the standard 50,257 50{,}257 -token GPT-2 tokenizer because rarely trained tokens distort the preconditioned curvature. Under Adam, the second-moment estimate of an embedding row grows with how often its token is trained on, so a token that is seldom seen has v ^ \sqrt{\hat{v}} close to the floor set by ϵ \epsilon . When such a token appears in the batch used for the Hessian-vector products, its row is amplified by roughly 1 / v ^ 1/\sqrt{\hat{v}} and can dominate the top eigenvalues. A smaller vocabulary leaves fewer such tokens. With 8,192 8{,}192 tokens, at most 72 72 tokens are rare by the criterion below at the checkpoints we used to build the filter. Even with the smaller vocabulary, we remove the remaining rare tokens from the data used for EoS and EoC detection. All detection batches come from a single training shard that no run is trained on. For a run with batch size B B at checkpoint step K K , we call a token rare if it has not appeared in the first K K training steps, if it has appeared less than once per step on average, or if it has not appeared in the last 20 20 steps. The padding token is always treated as rare. We take the union of the rare sets over the stable-phase checkpoints of all three model sizes ( 72 72 tokens) and drop every sequence of the shard whose inputs or targets contain a rare token. We also drop every sequence in which a token that appears fewer than 100 100 times per training step occurs more than 32 32 times, because such a burst over-represents that token’s row in a single batch. The filtered shard keeps 92,060 92{,}060 of 97,656 97{,}656 sequences ( 94.3 % 94.3\% ), and the same shard is used for every model size, learning rate and checkpoint. For model architectures, we apply QK-normalization ( Henry et al., 2020 ) and attention gating ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) for stability. All models are trained with a sequence length of 1024. We run most experiments on GPT-extra-small. Unless otherwise specified, we use 100 stochastic power iterations and 50 compensated local simulation steps for GPT-extra-small. For the larger models (GPT-small/medium/large), we use 50 power iterations and 25 local simulation steps. In all local simulations, we mark a run as exploding when the displacement norm reaches the cutoff M = 10 5 M=10^{5} .

sections.heading: EoS across the pretraining runs.
sections.text: The bounded-to-exploding transition of the compensated local simulation appears throughout our AdamW pretraining runs. Across models from 43M to 787M parameters, Figures 2 and 8 show many checkpoints at which the local simulation changes sharply from bounded trajectories to explosion near LR factor 1 1 . Figures 3 and 8 show that the location and duration of this behavior depend on the LR schedule and the peak LR. Figures 4 and 9 show that it also depends on the batch size. Taken together, these experiments show that EoS is common in our AdamW pretraining runs, and absent at the smallest batch size and extreme peak LRs. Within the LR range tested around the training LR, the simulations show one transition at most checkpoints. Under the assumptions of Theorem C.7 , strict homogeneous stability holds on a single LR interval whose endpoint is the AGM critical LR ( Proposition A.3 ).

sections.heading: Robustness to the compensation coefficient.
sections.text: Figure 10 shows one checkpoint with three compensation coefficients. The sharp transition is absent without compensation, appears at the estimated value, and remains visible at the larger value 600 600 .

sections.heading: B.3 Batch Size Threshold Experiments
sections.text: This subsection gives the protocol behind Section 6.3 . We study five datasets (FineWeb ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) , OpenWebMath ( Paster et al., 2024 ) , OpenWebText ( Gokaslan & Cohen, 2019 ) , C4 ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) , and DCLM ( Li et al., 2024 ) ) using GPT-extra-small. We use AdamW and the WSD schedule throughout, with baseline weight decay λ WD = 0.1 \lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}=0.1 . To vary the batch size, we follow the square-root scaling rule ( Malladi et al., 2022 ) . When increasing the batch size from B B to k ​ B kB , we scale the LR and the weight decay, keeping the remaining hyperparameters fixed, η ← k ​ η , λ WD ← k ​ λ WD , \eta\leftarrow\sqrt{k}\,\eta,\qquad\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}\leftarrow\sqrt{k}\,\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}, so that the timescale B / ( η ​ λ WD ) B/(\eta\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}) is the same for all batch sizes. We also adjust the second-moment decay coefficient β 2 \beta_{2} following Marek et al. (2025) : β 2 ← β 2 k . \beta_{2}\leftarrow\beta_{2}^{k}.

sections.heading: CBZ estimation.
sections.text: For each dataset, we sweep the batch size under this scaling rule and record the final evaluation loss of each run. We estimate the CBZ discussed in Section 6.3 as the largest batch size whose final evaluation loss stays within 0.3 % 0.3\% of the best loss over the sweep.

sections.heading: EBZ estimation.
sections.text: For each batch size B B , we estimate the critical LR ratio q = η ^ ⋆ / η q=\widehat{\eta}_{\star}/\eta defined in Section 6.3 , averaged over checkpoints. Runs whose local simulations stay bounded over the whole LR-factor grid are recorded as censored at the top of the grid. We then fit the averaged ratio as a function of B B . The EBZ of Section 6.3 is the smallest B B at which the fitted curve reaches 1.1 1.1 . Figure 4(a) compares EBZ to CBZ. Across the five datasets, EBZ and CBZ are strongly positively correlated (Pearson correlation 0.95 0.95 ). EBZ is below CBZ for C4 and FineWeb and above it for OpenWebMath, DCLM, and OpenWebText, so neither threshold is uniformly smaller.

sections.heading: Abrupt LR drops.
sections.text: We evaluate multistep schedule variants in Figure 11 . Before the drop, all six runs are at EoS ( 0.9 ≤ q ≤ 1.1 0.9\leq q\leq 1.1 ) at most checkpoints, 8 8 of the 9 9 checkpoints before the drop in panels a–c and 12 12 to 13 13 of the 14 14 in panels d–f. After the drop, the transition moves to larger LR factors, and EoS returns only when the LR after the drop stays large. With the peak LR fixed at 0.002 0.002 , no checkpoint after the drop is at EoS for any of the drop ratios 0.6 0.6 , 0.45 0.45 , and 0.3 0.3 (panels a–c). The median q q after the drop is 1.3 1.3 for the ratio 0.6 0.6 and 1.4 1.4 for 0.45 0.45 . For the ratio 0.3 0.3 , no LR factor in the grid explodes at 35 35 of the 41 41 checkpoints after the drop. With the drop ratio fixed at 0.7 0.7 (panels d–f), EoS returns at 26 26 of the 36 36 checkpoints after the drop for the peak LR 0.008 0.008 , at 7 7 for 0.004 0.004 , and at none for 0.0005 0.0005 .

sections.heading: Appendix C Theoretical Analysis
sections.text: This appendix studies optimization dynamics on quadratic approximations of the loss around a fixed training checkpoint, with the preconditioner held fixed. We describe how the mean and second moment of the state (momentum and parameter displacement) evolve from step to step, and present stability thresholds and error bounds for the EoC and EoS detectors. Proofs are in Appendices D , E and F .

sections.heading: C.2 Stability of the Local Dynamics
sections.text: Negative effective curvature makes the local dynamics unstable at every positive LR. On the strictly positive subspace, the LRs for strict homogeneous stability form a single interval.

sections.heading: Negative curvature.
sections.text: The first instability mode does not depend on the LR. Write 𝑫 = 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝑫 ℬ t ] {\bm{D}}=\mathbb{E}[{\bm{D}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}] for the population preconditioned Hessian ( 𝑫 t 0 {\bm{D}}_{t_{0}} in Section A.1 ). Lemma C.5 (Negative effective curvature) . Let Assumption C.1 hold. If the effective curvature 𝐀 = 𝐃 + λ WD ​ 𝐈 {\bm{A}}={\bm{D}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}{\bm{I}} has a negative eigenvalue, then the homogeneous AGM dynamics 𝐳 t + 1 = 𝐌 t ​ ( η ) ​ 𝐳 t {\bm{z}}_{t+1}={\bm{M}}_{t}(\eta){\bm{z}}_{t} of Proposition C.2 are not mean-square stable for any η > 0 \eta>0 . Along an eigendirection of 𝑫 {\bm{D}} with negative effective curvature, the mean dynamics reduce to a 2 × 2 2\times 2 system with a real eigenvalue above one for every η > 0 \eta>0 . Momentum changes the rate of growth, not its existence. A smaller LR slows the escape and does not prevent it. For SGD the rate is explicit. Write 𝑯 t 0 = ∇ 2 ℒ ​ ( 𝒘 t 0 ) {\bm{H}}_{t_{0}}=\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}(\bm{w}_{t_{0}}) for the population Hessian at the checkpoint. Corollary C.6 (Negative-curvature divergence) . Under the assumptions of Corollary C.4 , suppose 𝐇 t 0 {\bm{H}}_{t_{0}} has a unit eigenvector 𝐮 {\bm{u}} with eigenvalue λ < 0 \lambda<0 . The population quadratic is unbounded below. For every η > 0 \eta>0 , 𝒖 ⊤ ​ 𝔼 ​ [ 𝒘 t 0 + t − 𝒘 ⋆ ] = ( 1 − η ​ λ ) t ​ 𝒖 ⊤ ​ 𝔼 ​ [ 𝒘 t 0 − 𝒘 ⋆ ] . {\bm{u}}^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\bm{w}_{t_{0}+t}-\bm{w}_{\star}]=(1-\eta\lambda)^{t}\,{\bm{u}}^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\bm{w}_{t_{0}}-\bm{w}_{\star}]. Thus the mean diverges whenever the initial mean has a nonzero component along 𝐮 {\bm{u}} . The homogeneous system is not mean-square stable. This is the negative-curvature failure of Section 4.1 , now for the surrogate of a checkpoint. The proofs of the lemma and the corollary are in Section D.4 .

sections.heading: Mean-square and almost-sure stability.
sections.text: Consider the homogeneous recursion ϵ t + 1 = 𝑴 t ​ ϵ t \bm{\epsilon}_{t+1}={\bm{M}}_{t}\bm{\epsilon}_{t} with i.i.d. 𝑴 t {\bm{M}}_{t} of finite second moment. Recall the strict notion of Section C.1 . The recursion is strictly mean-square stable if 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ ϵ t ‖ 2 ] → 0 \mathbb{E}[\|\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\|^{2}]\to 0 for every deterministic initial state, and this holds if and only if the second-moment map below has spectral radius less than one. The main-text definition ( Definition 4.1 ) asks only for a bounded second moment. The AGM critical LR in Definition A.2 uses this same notion. Proposition A.3 shows that its threshold agrees with the strict homogeneous threshold on the same positive-mean subspace. Boundedness at the endpoint may depend on affine forcing. The spectral analysis below and in Appendix F uses strict homogeneous stability. Exponential mean-square decay requires constants K < ∞ K<\infty and 0 < ϱ < 1 0<\varrho<1 such that 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ ϵ t ‖ 2 ] ≤ K ​ ϱ t ​ ‖ ϵ 0 ‖ 2 . \mathbb{E}[\|\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\|^{2}]\leq K\varrho^{t}\|\bm{\epsilon}_{0}\|^{2}. Since 𝑴 t {\bm{M}}_{t} is independent of ϵ t \bm{\epsilon}_{t} , the second moment 𝔼 ⁡ [ ϵ t ​ ϵ t ⊤ ] \mathbb{E}[\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\bm{\epsilon}_{t}^{\top}] evolves as 𝔼 ⁡ [ ϵ t + 1 ​ ϵ t + 1 ⊤ ] = 𝒯 ⁡ ( 𝔼 ⁡ [ ϵ t ​ ϵ t ⊤ ] ) \mathbb{E}[\bm{\epsilon}_{t+1}\bm{\epsilon}_{t+1}^{\top}]=\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{E}[\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\bm{\epsilon}_{t}^{\top}]) , where 𝒯 ⁡ ( 𝑿 ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝑴 t ​ 𝑿 ​ 𝑴 t ⊤ ] . \mathcal{T}({\bm{X}})=\mathbb{E}[{\bm{M}}_{t}{\bm{X}}{\bm{M}}_{t}^{\top}]. Its matrix representation is the 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝑴 t ⊗ 𝑴 t ] \mathbb{E}[{\bm{M}}_{t}\otimes{\bm{M}}_{t}] of Proposition C.3 , and strict mean-square stability is the spectral condition ρ ⁡ ( 𝒯 ) < 1 \rho(\mathcal{T})<1 . This characterization makes mean-square stability useful for analyzing SGD ( Wu et al., 2018 ; Ma & Ying, 2021 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Mulayoff & Michaeli, 2024 ) . Almost-sure stability requires ‖ ϵ t ‖ → 0 \|\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\|\to 0 with probability one. Its exponential version is governed by the top Lyapunov exponent of the random matrix product, lim sup t → ∞ 1 t log ∥ 𝑴 t − 1 ⋯ 𝑴 0 ∥ < 0 almost surely , \limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}\log\|{\bm{M}}_{t-1}\cdots{\bm{M}}_{0}\|<0\qquad\text{almost surely}, under the usual integrability conditions ( Furstenberg & Kesten, 1960 ; Bougerol et al., 2012 ) . The two notions are not equivalent. Exponential mean-square decay implies almost-sure exponential stability by Markov’s inequality and the Borel–Cantelli lemma. The converse is false because rare expanding trajectories can dominate the second moment without changing the behavior of a typical sample path. For example, consider the scalar recursion ε t + 1 = a t ​ ε t \varepsilon_{t+1}=a_{t}\varepsilon_{t} , where the a t a_{t} are i.i.d. and a t = { 1 / 2 , with probability ​ 0.99 , 10 , with probability ​ 0.01 . a_{t}=\begin{cases}1/2,&\text{with probability }0.99,\\ 10,&\text{with probability }0.01.\end{cases} Here 𝔼 ⁡ [ log ⁡ a t ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\log a_{t}] = 0.99 ​ log ⁡ 1 2 + 0.01 ​ log ⁡ 10 ≈ − 0.66 < 0 , \displaystyle=0.99\log\tfrac{1}{2}+0.01\log 10\approx-0.66<0, 𝔼 ⁡ [ a t 2 ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[a_{t}^{2}] = 0.99 ⋅ 1 4 + 0.01 ⋅ 100 = 1.2475 > 1 . \displaystyle=0.99\cdot\tfrac{1}{4}+0.01\cdot 100=1.2475>1. Since log ⁡ | ε t | = log ⁡ | ε 0 | + ∑ s = 0 t − 1 log ⁡ a s \log|\varepsilon_{t}|=\log|\varepsilon_{0}|+\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}\log a_{s} , the strong law of large numbers gives 1 t ​ log ⁡ | ε t | → 𝔼 ⁡ [ log ⁡ a t ] < 0 \tfrac{1}{t}\log|\varepsilon_{t}|\to\mathbb{E}[\log a_{t}]<0 almost surely, so | ε t | → 0 |\varepsilon_{t}|\to 0 almost surely, whereas 𝔼 ⁡ [ | ε t | 2 ] = 𝔼 ​ [ a t 2 ] t ​ | ε 0 | 2 \mathbb{E}[|\varepsilon_{t}|^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[a_{t}^{2}]^{\,t}\,|\varepsilon_{0}|^{2} by independence, so 𝔼 ⁡ [ | ε t | 2 ] \mathbb{E}[|\varepsilon_{t}|^{2}] grows exponentially. The second moment can therefore reveal growth that an almost-sure criterion does not detect. We use mean-square stability because it controls the expected perturbation energy and admits a closed second-moment recursion. The experiments use a single-trajectory diagnostic, whose threshold need not coincide with this population threshold.

sections.heading: C.3 Stochastic Power Iteration for EoC
sections.text: We state the accuracy of the stochastic power iteration of Section A.2 . The theorem separates the error due to the finite horizon, the curvature noise, and the bisection resolution.

sections.heading: The system.
sections.text: We use the effective curvature of Section C.2 , writing the population preconditioned Hessian as 𝑫 t 0 {\bm{D}}_{t_{0}} , the 𝑫 {\bm{D}} of that section: 𝑨 \displaystyle{\bm{A}} ≔ 𝑫 t 0 + λ WD ​ 𝑰 , \displaystyle\coloneqq{\bm{D}}_{t_{0}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}{\bm{I}}, 𝑨 ℬ t \displaystyle{\bm{A}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}} ≔ 𝑷 − 1 / 2 𝑯 ℬ t 𝑷 − 1 / 2 + λ WD 𝑰 , \displaystyle\coloneqq{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}{\bm{H}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}{\bm{P}}^{-1/2}+\lambda_{\mathrm{WD}}{\bm{I}}, 𝚫 t \displaystyle{\bm{\Delta}}_{t} ≔ 𝑨 ℬ t − 𝑨 . \displaystyle\coloneqq{\bm{A}}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}-{\bm{A}}. Thus the deterministic weight-decay term is included in both curvatures and cancels from the noise 𝚫 t {\bm{\Delta}}_{t} . sections.heading: C.4 Compensated Local Simulation for EoS
sections.text: Our goal is to estimate the critical LR η ⋆ \eta_{\star} used to define EoS. The detector runs a compensated local model for only T T steps. Compensation changes the system being tested, whose critical LR we denote by η ⋆ 𝖯 \eta_{\star}^{\mathsf{P}} , and a finite simulation can accept LRs above this threshold. Theorem C.16 bounds the resulting error of the expected detector by accounting for these two effects. We first specify the systems and the detector, then introduce the quantities needed to bound each error.

sections.heading: Appendix D Proofs for the Local Linear System and the Stability Results
sections.text: This appendix proves the statements of Sections C.1 and C.2 in the order they are stated. Section D.1 derives the augmented linear system ( Proposition C.2 ) and its compensated form. Section D.2 derives the moment recursion of a stochastic linear system ( Proposition C.3 ). Section D.3 derives the moment recursion for SGD ( Corollary C.4 ) from the two propositions. Section D.4 proves the two negative-curvature results ( Lemmas C.5 and C.6 ) and Section D.5 the divergence above the critical LR ( Corollary C.8 ). Theorem C.7 is restated from Corollary F.4 and proved in Section F.5.3 . Section D.6 proves that bounded affine stability gives the same critical LR as the spectral criterion ( Proposition A.3 ). Throughout, ρ \rho denotes the spectral radius and ∥ ⋅ ∥ \|\cdot\| the spectral norm. We use gray text to indicate the identity, definition, or assumption used in each step of the derivation.

sections.heading: Appendix F Proof of the Compensated Finite-Horizon Threshold Bound
sections.text: In this appendix, we give the detailed proof of Theorem C.16 . The proof compares the projected critical LR, the compensated critical LR, and the finite-horizon detector output. Section F.1 gives the stability results used in this comparison. Section F.2 then proves the main bound from one compensation bound and one horizon bound. We prove these two bounds in Sections F.3 and F.4 . The proofs of the stability results and the auxiliary matrix facts follow in Sections F.5 and F.6 .

sections.text: The proofs use four finite-dimensional lemmas on second-moment maps and on maps that preserve positive semidefinite matrices. We also use the Cauchy–Schwarz and Minkowski inequalities, Jensen’s inequality, the Neumann series for ( s ​ ℐ − 𝒰 ) − 1 (s\mathcal{I}-\mathcal{U})^{-1} when | s | > ρ ⁡ ( 𝒰 ) |s|>\rho(\mathcal{U}) , the Rayleigh quotient characterization of the largest eigenvalue of a self-adjoint operator, and continuity of polynomial roots in their coefficients. The cutoff argument uses the Jordan decomposition: the powers of a finite-dimensional operator with spectral radius one grow at most polynomially. We distinguish two notions of positivity. A map 𝒰 : 𝕊 n → 𝕊 n \mathcal{U}:\mathbb{S}_{n}\to\mathbb{S}_{n} preserves PSD matrices if 𝑿 ⪰ 0 {\bm{X}}\succeq 0 implies 𝒰 ⁡ ( 𝑿 ) ⪰ 0 \mathcal{U}({\bm{X}})\succeq 0 . A self-adjoint operator 𝒟 \mathcal{D} on 𝕊 n \mathbb{S}_{n} is positive definite , written 𝒟 ≻ 0 \mathcal{D}\succ 0 , if ⟨ 𝑿 , 𝒟 ​ 𝑿 ⟩ > 0 \left\langle{{\bm{X}}},{\mathcal{D}{\bm{X}}}\right\rangle>0 for every nonzero symmetric 𝑿 {\bm{X}} . Preservation of PSD matrices does not imply positive definiteness as an operator, and the converse fails as well. Second moments are uncentered throughout: 𝚺 t = 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝒚 t ​ 𝒚 t ⊤ ] {\bm{\Sigma}}_{t}=\mathbb{E}[{\bm{y}}_{t}{\bm{y}}_{t}^{\top}] , so that tr ⁡ 𝚺 t = 𝔼 ​ ‖ 𝒚 t ‖ 2 \tr{\bm{\Sigma}}_{t}=\mathbb{E}\left\|{\bm{y}}_{t}\right\|^{2} , and no zero-mean assumption is imposed on the state.
